Building on this network view, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance in a heart failure context. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the proteins listed, TREM2 stands out as the most compelling candidate for relevance to heart failure because it is centrally involved in innate immune activation, macrophage biology, phagocytosis, and inflammatory regulation, all of which are major determinants of cardiac remodeling and progression to heart failure. Heart failure is increasingly recognized as a syndrome driven not only by hemodynamic stress but also by persistent sterile inflammation, recruitment of myeloid cells, defective clearance of dying cells, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. TREM2-associated signaling is particularly relevant in this context because it regulates activation of monocyte and macrophage lineage cells, promotes phagocytosis of apoptotic cells, and modulates cytokine responses. These functions may influence post-injury resolution pathways after myocardial infarction, as well as chronic inflammatory remodeling in non-ischemic heart failure. Its documented roles in promoting cell activation through receptor complexes, supporting dendritic cell maturation and survival, regulating interleukin 10 production, and controlling pro-inflammatory responses suggest that altered TREM2 activity could shape the balance between reparative and maladaptive cardiac inflammation. In addition, its role in multinucleation and osteoclast cytoskeletal organization underscores a broader function in myeloid cell differentiation and fusion, processes mechanistically related to macrophage activation states that can affect fibrotic remodeling. Thus, although the provided annotations do not mention the heart directly, TREM2 appears strongly connected to disease mechanisms that are highly pertinent to heart failure pathogenesis, especially immune-cell-driven remodeling and inflammatory injury.[PubMed:15471863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15471863) [PubMed:9647200](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9647200) [PubMed:15728241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728241) [PubMed:16715077](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16715077) [PubMed:21727189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21727189) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:18957693](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18957693) [PubMed:18685038](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18685038) [PubMed:25690660](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25690660) [PubMed:21257958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21257958) [PubMed:18691974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18691974) [PubMed:12569157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12569157) [PubMed:14969392](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14969392) 

A related but distinct aspect of this pathway involves lysosomal antigen processing, which makes IFI30 a plausible protein of interest in this setting. IFI30 is relevant to heart failure because it links lysosomal processing, antigen presentation, and adaptive immune activation. In many forms of heart failure, especially after myocardial infarction, myocarditis, or chronic cardiometabolic injury, damaged cardiac tissue releases intracellular and matrix-derived antigens that can be taken up by antigen-presenting cells. IFI30 enhances the processing of structurally complex antigens containing disulfide bonds, thereby facilitating major histocompatibility complex class two presentation to cluster of differentiation four positive T cells and cross-presentation to cluster of differentiation eight positive T cells. This is potentially important in heart failure because persistent antigen presentation can sustain myocardial inflammation, amplify autoimmune-like responses against cardiac antigens, and worsen adverse remodeling. In addition, IFI30-dependent lysosomal reduction is consistent with a broader role in macrophage and dendritic cell function, which are central regulators of post-injury repair, fibrosis, and ventricular remodeling. Therefore, IFI30 stands out as a plausible contributor to immune-mediated mechanisms of heart failure progression through its effects on antigen processing and T-cell activation.

In parallel with antigen-presenting cell biology, humoral immune regulation may also contribute to this broader inflammatory landscape, which brings FCER2 into consideration. FCER2 is of interest in heart failure primarily because it connects B-cell biology, antigen presentation, immunoglobulin E-associated immunity, and nitric oxide-linked macrophage effector responses. Although its canonical role is in allergic and antiparasitic immunity, several of its functions are mechanistically relevant to cardiovascular disease. B cells are increasingly implicated in heart failure through antibody production, cytokine secretion, and modulation of inflammatory remodeling, and FCER2 contributes directly to B-cell differentiation and antigen presentation to T cells. These properties suggest that it could participate in immune amplification within chronic inflammatory states that predispose to or worsen heart failure. Moreover, its ability to trigger macrophage L-arginine to nitric oxide pathway activity is notable because nitric oxide signaling is deeply involved in vascular tone regulation, myocardial energetics, inflammatory injury, and endothelial dysfunction, all of which influence heart failure pathophysiology. While the evidence from the provided annotation is indirect, FCER2 may be relevant particularly in inflammatory or immune-mediated forms of cardiac dysfunction where B-cell activation and macrophage signaling contribute to disease progression.

Beyond immune signaling itself, intracellular trafficking pathways may also shape how stressed cardiac cells respond to injury, making RAB6A potentially relevant. RAB6A is potentially relevant to heart failure because intracellular membrane trafficking and Golgi to endoplasmic reticulum communication are essential for cardiomyocyte proteostasis, receptor turnover, and stress adaptation. Heart failure is characterized by major disturbances in protein quality control, secretory pathway function, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and maladaptive remodeling of membrane systems. As a regulator of Golgi-to-endoplasmic reticulum retrograde transport, RAB6A may influence the recovery and recycling of proteins required for cellular homeostasis under stress conditions. In cardiomyocytes, such trafficking pathways are important for maintaining ion channel localization, membrane receptor signaling, sarcoplasmic and secretory protein processing, and adaptation to biomechanical load. Although the supplied annotation emphasizes neuronal development rather than cardiovascular biology, the core function of RAB6A in vesicular transport makes it biologically plausible as a modifier of heart failure through effects on cellular stress responses and proteostatic balance.

Finally, the interface between cellular stress and immune surveillance provides another potentially relevant connection to heart failure, represented here by ULBP2. ULBP2 is noteworthy in relation to heart failure because it represents a stress-induced immune recognition pathway that may link cellular injury to cytotoxic inflammation. The heart under ischemic, oxidative, viral, or metabolic stress may express ligands that activate innate and adaptive immune surveillance pathways. As a natural killer group two member D ligand, ULBP2 can trigger natural killer cell activation and augment cluster of differentiation eight positive T-cell responses, leading to cytotoxic killing and inflammatory cytokine production. These mechanisms are relevant to heart failure in settings such as viral myocarditis, transplant-related injury, ischemia-reperfusion damage, and chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy, where stressed cardiac or vascular cells may become targets of immune-mediated injury. Its ability to promote tumor necrosis factor alpha expression is especially important because tumor necrosis factor alpha is a well-established mediator of adverse cardiac remodeling, contractile dysfunction, and progression of heart failure. Therefore, ULBP2 may be most relevant in forms of heart failure where tissue stress and immune cytotoxicity intersect.

### external encapsulating structure (GO:0030312) 

The pathway term external encapsulating structure refers to biological structures located outside the plasma membrane that surround the whole cell or groups of cells. In mammalian tissues, this concept is represented primarily by the extracellular matrix and closely related pericellular structures, including basement membrane, interstitial collagen networks, proteoglycan-rich matrices, and secreted adhesive glycoproteins. These structures are not passive coverings; rather, they provide biomechanical support, organize tissue architecture, regulate cell adhesion, and control the availability of growth factors, cytokines, and other signaling molecules. In the heart, the external encapsulating structure is essential for maintaining myocardial integrity because it coordinates interactions among cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and inflammatory cells. Remodeling of this extracellular environment can alter ventricular stiffness, microvascular function, mechanotransduction, oxidative stress responses, and inflammatory signaling, all of which are central processes in the development and progression of heart failure. Although several of the provided publications are not focused on cardiovascular disease, they collectively reinforce that genes assigned to this pathway are commonly linked to extracellular matrix organization, cell adhesion, barrier properties, and structural adaptation of tissues. The most directly relevant study identifies reelin as a secreted extracellular matrix protein involved in organizing the external encapsulating structure, thereby connecting this pathway to endothelial homeostasis and cardiac function in disease settings.  

Building on this conceptual framework, the relationship between the external encapsulating structure pathway and heart failure is supported most directly by evidence showing that disruption of extracellular matrix-associated endothelial signaling may worsen cardiac dysfunction. In the study of diabetic cardiomyopathy, endothelial reelin, described as a large secreted extracellular matrix protein critical for organizing the external encapsulating structure, was shown to protect the heart; endothelial-specific loss of reelin caused reduced ejection performance, impaired systolic structure and function, increased endothelial apoptosis, increased reactive oxygen species production, defective mitochondrial quality control, and enhanced inflammatory chemokine production, thereby accelerating cardiomyopathic remodeling that is highly relevant to heart failure pathogenesis. This finding suggests that proper organization of the extracellular environment surrounding cardiac endothelial cells may be necessary for preserving myocardial homeostasis and limiting progression toward pump failure. Additional support comes from the broader literature in the provided set showing that the external encapsulating structure category is strongly associated with extracellular matrix enrichment and tissue remodeling, as illustrated in keloid biology, where this term co-enriched with collagen-containing extracellular matrix and extracellular matrix programs, underscoring that pathway activation often reflects structural remodeling and fibrotic matrix deposition. In the context of heart failure, analogous extracellular matrix expansion and disorganization are established drivers of ventricular stiffening, impaired relaxation, capillary dysfunction, and chronic inflammation. Therefore, although the publication set contains only one directly cardiovascular study, the combined evidence supports a biologically coherent but still cautious interpretation: abnormalities in the external encapsulating structure pathway may contribute to heart failure by promoting maladaptive extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammatory signaling, and consequent deterioration of cardiac structure and performance, with especially strong relevance in metabolically stressed states such as diabetic heart disease.[PubMed:39952154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39952154) 

Extending from the literature-based interpretation to the enrichment results, there were 105 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway term external encapsulating structure, indicating a substantial concentration of disease-related proteins within a biological compartment that surrounds cells and tissues and is fundamentally involved in extracellular matrix organization, cell adhesion, tissue architecture, and structural adaptation. In the context of heart failure, an enrichment set of 105 proteins supports a broad systems-level involvement of extracellular and pericellular remodeling processes, consistent with the central contribution of matrix reorganization, ventricular stiffening, endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling, and altered biomechanical coupling to disease progression. The functional interpretation of this pathway is especially relevant because the external encapsulating structure includes basement membrane, interstitial collagen networks, proteoglycan-rich matrices, and secreted adhesive glycoproteins, all of which collectively regulate myocardial integrity and intercellular communication among cardiomyocytes, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and inflammatory cells. The size of the enriched protein set, comprising 105 proteins, further suggests that this signal is not driven by a small isolated module but instead reflects a large and biologically coherent extracellular program with potential impact on tissue mechanics, growth factor availability, oxidative stress responses, and microvascular homeostasis in heart failure. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 105 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection of the network topology and functional connectivity.

![PPI Network](imgs/8030c709-bdb2-4c4e-a237-24ece60f8f90.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=609DBBBA735A6969)

With this network-level context in mind, during the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

VEGFA is one of the most directly relevant proteins in the context of heart failure because myocardial adaptation to stress critically depends on vascular integrity, endothelial survival, and sufficient capillary density. Impaired angiogenic signaling contributes to myocardial ischemia, maladaptive remodeling, fibrosis, and progression from compensated hypertrophy to overt heart failure. The described VEGFA receptor-mediated functions, including activation of AKT and MAPK survival pathways, reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, and induction of NOS2 and NOS3-dependent nitric oxide production, are highly pertinent to cardiac microvascular homeostasis and myocardial perfusion. In heart failure, endothelial dysfunction and capillary rarefaction are common features, and VEGFA-related signaling can influence both compensatory neovascularization and vascular permeability. Thus, this protein stands out as a mechanistically important node linking vascular biology, tissue oxygen delivery, and remodeling responses in failing myocardium.  

Closely related to this vascular theme, EGFL7 is highly relevant to heart failure because it integrates endothelial organization with vascular remodeling. In the failing heart, microvascular dysfunction, aberrant endothelial repair, and pathological vascular remodeling contribute to reduced tissue perfusion and progressive myocardial injury. EGFL7 promotes endothelial adhesion and angiogenesis while restraining smooth muscle cell migration, suggesting a role in maintaining vessel architecture and limiting maladaptive vascular thickening. These properties are especially important in the setting of pressure overload, ischemic injury, or inflammatory remodeling, where preservation of a functional microcirculation may influence ventricular recovery and fibrosis. Its emphasis on vascular tubulogenesis makes EGFL7 particularly notable among the listed proteins as a candidate mediator of adaptive versus maladaptive cardiac vascular remodeling.  

From vascular organization, the analysis also shifts toward metabolic regulation, where ANGPTL4 appears important for heart failure biology because disordered lipid metabolism is a major contributor to cardiometabolic stress, especially in obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome-associated heart failure. By inhibiting LPL, ANGPTL4 directly controls triglyceride utilization and circulating lipid handling. This is relevant to the myocardium, which relies heavily on fatty acid metabolism and is highly sensitive to lipotoxicity, substrate imbalance, and energetic inefficiency. Altered ANGPTL4 activity may therefore influence systemic metabolic load as well as cardiac fuel availability. In addition, dyslipidemia and endothelial dysfunction frequently coexist in heart failure, making ANGPTL4 a plausible link between metabolic derangement and vascular injury. Its strong mechanistic connection to triglyceride clearance makes it one of the more compelling proteins in this list for heart failure, particularly in metabolically driven disease.[PubMed:19270337](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19270337) [PubMed:21398697](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21398697) [PubMed:27929370](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27929370) [PubMed:29899144](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29899144) 

A related but more systemic dimension is represented by GDF15, which is particularly noteworthy in heart failure because it is a well-recognized systemic stress-response factor and is strongly associated clinically with adverse cardiovascular outcomes, cachexia, and disease severity. The function provided here emphasizes its role in stress-induced aversive signaling, appetite suppression, and metabolic adaptation through GFRAL-RET signaling. These features are highly relevant to advanced heart failure, where chronic inflammation, neurohormonal activation, and catabolic stress frequently culminate in anorexia, weight loss, and frailty. Although the canonical receptor system is localized to the brainstem, the downstream physiological consequences, including reduced food intake, altered energy balance, and stress adaptation, fit closely with mechanisms underlying cardiac cachexia and poor prognosis in heart failure populations. Therefore, GDF15 stands out less as a structural cardiac effector and more as a biomarker-linked mediator of systemic disease burden in heart failure.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

In parallel with these systemic stress signals, MDK emerges as one of the most compelling proteins in relation to heart failure because it sits at the intersection of inflammation, angiogenesis, tissue repair, and fibrosis-related remodeling. The listed functions indicate that MDK recruits neutrophils and macrophages, promotes cell survival via MAPK and AKT pathways, supports angiogenesis, and participates in tissue regeneration after injury, including heart damage. These processes are fundamental to post-injury ventricular remodeling and to the transition from acute damage to chronic heart failure. Its ability to influence inflammatory cell trafficking may be beneficial in repair but may also drive persistent inflammatory remodeling if dysregulated. Furthermore, its effects on endothelial biology, smooth muscle behavior, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition suggest broader relevance to vascular remodeling and fibrosis. Because heart failure progression depends heavily on the balance between reparative and maladaptive remodeling, MDK stands out as a multifunctional mediator with plausible pathogenic and compensatory roles.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

This inflammatory and metabolic interface also makes RARRES2 relevant to heart failure because it links adipose dysfunction, systemic inflammation, insulin resistance, and vascular biology, which are four major determinants of cardiometabolic heart failure. Its dual pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory properties are especially interesting. On one hand, it can promote inflammatory adipokine release and worsen metabolic dysfunction, both of which are strongly implicated in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity-related cardiac disease. On the other hand, it can suppress TNF-induced VCAM1 expression and monocyte adhesion in endothelial cells via AKT1 and NOS3 signaling, indicating a potential protective effect on vascular inflammation. This functional duality mirrors the complex inflammatory-metabolic milieu observed in heart failure. RARRES2 therefore stands out as a plausible mediator connecting adipose tissue signaling to endothelial dysfunction, immune activation, and systemic metabolic stress in heart failure.  

Moving from inflammatory signaling to direct matrix degradation, PRTN3 is relevant to heart failure because extracellular matrix turnover, vascular inflammation, and leukocyte trafficking are central components of adverse cardiac remodeling. Its ability to degrade elastin, fibronectin, laminin, vitronectin, and collagens suggests a direct capacity to influence matrix integrity, which is highly pertinent to ventricular dilation, fibrosis, and tissue injury after cardiac stress. At the same time, its role in neutrophil transendothelial migration and inflammatory activation indicates a contribution to innate immune responses that can either support acute repair or exacerbate chronic myocardial damage. Since inflammatory cell infiltration and matrix remodeling are key drivers of post-infarction remodeling and progressive heart failure, PRTN3 stands out as a protein with credible mechanistic links to both vascular and extracellular matrix pathology.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

Consistent with the importance of matrix remodeling, CTHRC1 is potentially important in heart failure because excessive collagen accumulation and interstitial fibrosis are major determinants of ventricular stiffening, impaired relaxation, arrhythmogenic substrate formation, and progression to both preserved-ejection fraction and reduced-ejection fraction heart failure. A protein that negatively regulates collagen matrix deposition could influence the balance between necessary scar formation and maladaptive fibrosis. Although the functional annotation here is concise, the implication is substantial: altered CTHRC1 expression or activity could modify extracellular matrix remodeling after myocardial injury or during chronic pressure overload. This makes CTHRC1 a notable candidate in pathways governing fibrotic burden and structural remodeling in heart failure.  

Another extracellular matrix-associated candidate is TNC, which is highly relevant to heart failure because it is an extracellular matrix-associated signaling molecule with recognized roles in tissue remodeling and cell-matrix communication. Its integrin-binding properties and ability to stimulate endothelial migration and sprouting suggest a role in remodeling of the cardiac interstitium and vasculature after injury. In the heart, matricellular proteins often become re-expressed during stress and modulate inflammation, fibroblast activation, angiogenesis, and mechanical adaptation of the extracellular matrix. TNC therefore stands out as a plausible mediator of post-injury remodeling, particularly where extracellular matrix reorganization and repair-associated angiogenesis determine whether the ventricle undergoes adaptive healing or progressive dysfunction.[PubMed:19884327](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19884327) 

In addition to structural remodeling, pathway regulation is also represented by SFRP1, which is notable in heart failure because Wnt and beta-catenin signaling is a major pathway in cardiac development, fibroblast activation, vascular remodeling, and post-injury repair. By antagonizing Wnt signaling and lowering beta-catenin levels, SFRP1 may affect the balance between regeneration and fibrosis. Its antiproliferative effects on vascular cells also suggest relevance to remodeling of the cardiac vasculature. In heart failure, aberrant Wnt activation has been implicated in maladaptive hypertrophy and fibrotic remodeling; accordingly, proteins such as SFRP1 that modulate this pathway are of substantial interest. The combination of Wnt regulation and vascular effects makes SFRP1 a mechanistically meaningful candidate in the progression of structural heart disease.  

At a broader signaling level, LRIG1 is relevant to heart failure because receptor tyrosine kinase signaling governs cardiomyocyte survival, growth, endothelial repair, and fibrotic responses. A negative regulator such as LRIG1 may attenuate excessive growth factor signaling, which can be beneficial by limiting maladaptive remodeling, but could also impair reparative responses if overactive. Since pathways driven by receptor tyrosine kinases, including those related to epidermal growth factor receptor, vascular endothelial growth factor family receptors, and other growth factor systems, are central to myocardial stress adaptation and vascular maintenance, LRIG1 may influence the threshold between adaptive signaling and pathological remodeling. Its broad regulatory role makes it a potentially important upstream modulator rather than a single-pathway effector in heart failure biology.  

A related extracellular component is SMOC2, which is of interest in heart failure because it combines extracellular matrix regulatory activity with pro-angiogenic effects. Cardiac remodeling involves both matrix reorganization and vascular adaptation, and proteins that influence these processes may determine ventricular stiffness, tissue repair quality, and perfusion. By promoting matrix assembly, SMOC2 may contribute to structural remodeling, while its stimulation of endothelial proliferation and migration suggests a role in compensatory neovascularization. This dual function is particularly relevant in the stressed myocardium, where the interplay between fibrosis and angiogenesis strongly shapes disease progression.  

Similarly, CCDC80 is potentially relevant to heart failure because cell adhesion and extracellular matrix assembly are fundamental determinants of myocardial architecture and mechanical performance. Heart failure is characterized by extensive remodeling of the interstitial matrix, altered force transmission, and changes in fibroblast-matrix interactions. Although the annotation is brief, proteins that promote matrix assembly may influence fibrosis, tissue stiffness, and structural integrity of the ventricle. CCDC80 therefore stands out as a plausible extracellular remodeling factor that may affect disease progression through matrix organization.  

Finally, VWA1 may have indirect relevance to heart failure through its role in matrix assembly and muscle organization. Although the annotation emphasizes skeletal muscle, extracellular matrix organizing proteins often have broader roles in tissue mechanics and repair. In heart failure, matrix disorganization contributes to impaired contractility and ventricular remodeling, while skeletal muscle abnormalities also affect exercise capacity and clinical status. Therefore, VWA1 is noteworthy as a candidate linked to structural matrix biology and potentially to the peripheral muscle dysfunction that accompanies chronic heart failure.

### glycosaminoglycan binding (GO:0005539) 

Glycosaminoglycan binding refers to the selective interaction of proteins with sulfated polysaccharides such as heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and related extracellular matrix or cell-surface glycans that are enriched in amino sugars. In biological systems, this interaction is typically mediated by clusters of positively charged amino acid residues on the binding protein and serves several fundamental functions, including immobilization of soluble mediators on endothelial and stromal surfaces, shaping of concentration gradients, modulation of ligand stability, control of receptor accessibility, and organization of extracellular signaling microenvironments. The publications provided indicate that glycosaminoglycan binding is particularly important for chemokine biology. Matrix metalloproteinase processing can increase the glycosaminoglycan-binding properties of chemokines, as demonstrated for chemokine ligand sixteen, thereby altering inflammatory cell recruitment potential and tissue localization. Other studies further show that chemokine function can be amplified or restrained through glycosaminoglycan interactions: chemokine ligand seven uses multiple glycosaminoglycan-binding epitopes to maintain surface association, chemokine ligand eighteen can inhibit leukocyte recruitment by displacing glycosaminoglycan-bound chemokines, chemokine ligand seven shares overlapping receptor- and heparin-binding surfaces, and a carboxyl-terminal peptide derived from chemokine ligand nine suppresses inflammation by competing for glycosaminoglycan binding. In addition, glycosaminoglycan engagement on endothelial cells is not merely passive tethering; it can trigger downstream endothelial responses, including altered expression of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion, and mobility, with syndecan four identified as a likely co-receptor for chemokine ligand eight. Collectively, this pathway appears to represent a central extracellular regulatory system that integrates matrix composition, protease activity, endothelial activation, and leukocyte trafficking.

Building on these mechanistic observations, the potential relevance of this pathway to heart failure can be considered in a cautious but biologically grounded manner. Although none of the cited studies examined heart failure directly, they define mechanisms that are highly relevant to heart failure pathogenesis because heart failure is characterized by chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial dysfunction, and maladaptive immune cell recruitment. A central implication of glycosaminoglycan binding in this disease context is that it governs how inflammatory chemokines are retained, presented, and function within injured cardiac tissue and the activated vascular endothelium. The study of matrix metalloproteinase processing of monocyte-directed chemokines showed that proteolysis can generate more potent inflammatory ligands and can enhance glycosaminoglycan binding, as seen for chemokine ligand sixteen, thereby increasing the likelihood of persistent chemokine immobilization and monocyte recruitment in inflamed tissues; this mechanism is especially pertinent to heart failure, where matrix metalloproteinases and monocyte-macrophage accumulation are well-established features of adverse remodeling (PubMed:22147696). The work on chemokine ligand seven further indicates that glycosaminoglycan density regulates chemokine accumulation on cell surfaces, suggesting that remodeling of the cardiac extracellular matrix and endothelial glycocalyx in heart failure could directly alter chemokine gradient formation and inflammatory cell trafficking (PubMed:24727473). The endothelial signaling study provides an additional layer of relevance by showing that chemokine binding to endothelial glycosaminoglycans can modify endothelial protein programs linked to adhesion and cytoskeletal dynamics, implying that glycosaminoglycan-dependent signaling may contribute to vascular activation, leukocyte transmigration, and microvascular dysfunction in failing hearts (PubMed:29207576). Importantly, two studies support the concept that interference with chemokine-glycosaminoglycan interactions can suppress inflammation: chemokine ligand eighteen displaced glycosaminoglycan-bound chemokines and inhibited receptor-driven chemotaxis, while a glycosaminoglycan-binding peptide derived from chemokine ligand nine reduced neutrophil extravasation in vivo by competing for glycosaminoglycan occupancy (PubMed:23951310, PubMed:26183778). Together, these findings support a coherent model in which glycosaminoglycan binding may amplify and spatially organize inflammatory signaling in the heart and vasculature, thereby potentially promoting immune cell recruitment, endothelial activation, and extracellular matrix-driven remodeling that contribute to the initiation and progression of heart failure; conversely, disruption of this pathway may represent a plausible anti-inflammatory strategy in the disease.[PubMed:22147696](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22147696) [PubMed:24727473](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24727473) [PubMed:29207576](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29207576) [PubMed:23951310](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23951310) [PubMed:26183778](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26183778) [PubMed:28245630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28245630) 

This literature-based interpretation is also consistent with the enrichment pattern observed in the present dataset. There were 35 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of glycosaminoglycan binding, a functional category centered on the selective interaction of proteins with sulfated extracellular glycans such as heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, and dermatan sulfate. This enrichment indicates that a substantial protein set of 35 members converges on an extracellular regulatory mechanism that controls mediator retention, gradient formation, ligand stability, receptor accessibility, and spatial organization of signaling at endothelial and stromal surfaces. In the context of heart failure, the biological relevance of this pathway is quantitatively notable because it links extracellular matrix composition, proteolytic remodeling, endothelial activation, and leukocyte trafficking within a single enriched functional theme, suggesting that matrix-associated inflammatory signaling may represent a major component of disease-associated protein organization. The pathway description further indicates that glycosaminoglycan binding can reshape chemokine localization and potency through multiple mechanisms, including increased binding after matrix metalloproteinase processing, competition for glycosaminoglycan occupancy, overlap between receptor-binding and heparin-binding surfaces, and endothelial signaling effects involving cytoskeletal organization, adhesion, and mobility. Taken together, the enrichment of 35 proteins supports the interpretation that extracellular glycan-mediated signaling control is not a marginal feature but rather a quantitatively represented component of the heart failure-associated protein landscape.

To further contextualize this enrichment, we also include the protein-protein interaction network visualization for these 35 proteins together with the link to the STRING webpage for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/74585f19-6dec-4c0b-a017-82423bb0be03.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=B5D932863B3712F4)

With this network context in place, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance in a more focused manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

VEGFA stands out as one of the most directly relevant proteins to heart failure because impaired myocardial perfusion, endothelial dysfunction, microvascular rarefaction, and maladaptive vascular remodeling are core features of both ischemic and non-ischemic heart failure. The listed functions indicate that VEGFA controls endothelial survival and migration, vascular permeability, and nitric oxide signaling, all of which are highly pertinent to myocardial oxygen delivery and vascular homeostasis. Its activation of AKT, ERK, FAK, SRC, and NOS pathways further links it to cardioprotective signaling, angiogenic repair, and maintenance of vascular integrity. In the failing heart, insufficient angiogenic adaptation can worsen hypoxia and fibrosis, whereas dysregulated VEGFA signaling may also contribute to edema and abnormal vascular permeability. Thus, VEGFA appears highly relevant to heart-failure pathobiology through its integrated roles in angiogenesis, endothelial health, and tissue perfusion.

Closely related to this vascular and reparative theme, MDK also appears particularly compelling in the context of heart failure because its annotated functions explicitly include roles after cardiac injury. The protein promotes cell survival, angiogenesis, and tissue regeneration while modulating inflammatory-cell recruitment, processes that are central to post-injury remodeling and progression to heart failure. Its ability to activate MAPK and AKT signaling suggests a mechanistic basis for cardiomyocyte and vascular-cell protection, whereas its effects on macrophage and neutrophil recruitment indicate a role in shaping the inflammatory milieu that drives adverse remodeling. In addition, MDK can induce VEGFA expression and nitric oxide synthase activity during arteriogenesis, further linking it to vascular adaptation in the injured myocardium. Collectively, these properties make MDK a strong candidate mediator of the balance between reparative and maladaptive remodeling in heart failure.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) 

Extending this line of reasoning from vascular adaptation to direct myocardial protection, FSTL1 is highly relevant to heart failure because the provided annotation directly identifies a cardioprotective effect through promotion of cardiac myocyte survival. In parallel, its pro-angiogenic actions on endothelial cells suggest that it may support vascular maintenance and reparative neovascularization in the stressed or injured heart. These dual effects are important because heart failure progression is driven by both cardiomyocyte loss and impaired microvascular adaptation. The involvement of AKT-dependent signaling is especially noteworthy, as AKT is a well-established pro-survival pathway in cardiovascular biology. Furthermore, the link to immune regulation raises the possibility that FSTL1 modulates inflammatory remodeling, another key determinant of ventricular dysfunction. Overall, FSTL1 emerges as a strong heart-failure-related factor at the intersection of cardiomyocyte survival, endothelial repair, and inflammatory control.[PubMed:19595790](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19595790) [PubMed:20054002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20054002) [PubMed:21826198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21826198) 

Shifting from survival and angiogenesis to structural remodeling, TGFBR2 is one of the most important proteins for heart-failure relevance because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a central driver of fibrosis and adverse cardiac remodeling. The listed functions include regulation of extracellular matrix production, wound healing, mesenchymal-cell proliferation and differentiation, and apoptosis, all of which are fundamental to the structural remodeling that stiffens the ventricle and impairs systolic or diastolic function. Canonical SMAD signaling and non-canonical pathways downstream of TGFBR2 can promote fibroblast activation and matrix accumulation, thereby contributing to myocardial fibrosis, increased chamber stiffness, and progressive dysfunction. Its additional role in immunoregulation further supports relevance, as inflammatory-fibrotic crosstalk is a major determinant of heart-failure progression. Therefore, TGFBR2 represents a mechanistically central node linking injury responses to maladaptive remodeling.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) 

A closely related but somewhat broader regulatory component is TGFBR3, which is relevant to heart failure because it modulates transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein pathway activity, both of which are deeply involved in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, vascular biology, and repair responses. The annotation indicates effects on cell migration, adhesion, focal adhesion formation, and cytoskeletal organization, suggesting potential roles in fibroblast behavior, endothelial responses, and structural remodeling of cardiac tissue. Its interaction with nuclear factor kappa B-related signaling also connects it to inflammatory regulation, which is highly pertinent in chronic heart failure. In addition, modulation of actin dynamics and integrin signaling may influence mechanotransduction, an important process in the overloaded or injured myocardium. Although less directly heart-specific than TGFBR2, TGFBR3 stands out as a plausible regulator of fibrotic and vascular remodeling pathways relevant to disease progression.[PubMed:30364975](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30364975) [PubMed:34910520](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34910520) 

Moving from transforming growth factor beta pathway components to other extracellular growth modulators, FGFBP1 is notable in relation to heart failure because fibroblast growth factor signaling and integrin-mediated signaling are both relevant to cardiac repair, vascular remodeling, and endothelial adaptation. The ability of FGFBP1 to induce angiogenesis and regulate cell survival and migration suggests that it may influence myocardial vascularization and tissue responses to ischemic or hemodynamic stress. Its interaction with ITGAV:ITGB3 is particularly interesting because integrin signaling contributes to extracellular matrix sensing and remodeling, processes heavily implicated in ventricular remodeling. In a heart-failure setting, proteins that coordinate growth-factor and integrin pathways may affect the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive remodeling. Thus, FGFBP1 is a plausible contributor to vascular and stromal mechanisms underlying disease progression.[PubMed:8663044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [PubMed:28302677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [PubMed:1721615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [PubMed:3732516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [PubMed:3964259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [PubMed:23469107](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [PubMed:29501879](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879) 

In a similar extracellular remodeling context, THBS2 is relevant to heart failure because extracellular matrix remodeling and impaired angiogenesis are major contributors to ventricular dysfunction. As an adhesive matrix-associated glycoprotein with antiangiogenic activity through CD36, THBS2 may restrain capillary growth and thereby worsen microvascular insufficiency in the stressed myocardium. At the same time, its role in cell-matrix interactions suggests involvement in structural remodeling and matrix organization, processes that influence ventricular stiffness and scar formation. In the context of heart failure, excessive antiangiogenic signaling can limit compensatory vascularization, especially during hypertrophy or post-infarction repair. Therefore, THBS2 stands out as a plausible mediator linking extracellular matrix remodeling to impaired vascular adaptation.

Another extracellular regulator with potential relevance to remodeling is SFRP1, which is of interest for heart failure because Wnt and beta-catenin signaling is a recognized regulator of cardiac development, fibroblast activation, vascular remodeling, and post-injury repair. By decreasing beta-catenin levels and modulating WNT1 and WNT4-dependent transcription, SFRP1 may influence the fibrotic and proliferative responses that shape ventricular remodeling. Its reported antiproliferative effects on vascular cells also suggest a role in vascular homeostasis, although the net consequences may depend on context. Since maladaptive reactivation of developmental signaling pathways, including Wnt signaling, is a hallmark of failing myocardium, SFRP1 may act as an important extracellular regulator of these remodeling programs. This makes it a biologically plausible contributor to heart-failure progression or compensation.

Continuing with matrix-associated proteins that may bridge structural and vascular responses, SMOC2 is potentially relevant to heart failure because it integrates two disease-relevant processes: extracellular matrix organization and angiogenesis. Matrix assembly and altered cell adhesiveness are central to myocardial remodeling, while endothelial proliferation and migration are essential for adaptive vascular growth and tissue repair. In failing hearts, the balance between matrix deposition and vascular support is often disrupted, leading to fibrosis, capillary rarefaction, and progressive dysfunction. A protein such as SMOC2, which may influence both matrix and endothelial behavior, could therefore participate in the remodeling environment that determines disease severity. Its role may be especially pertinent in post-injury repair and chronic interstitial remodeling.

Within this broader extracellular matrix framework, PRELP may also be relevant to heart failure, although the connection appears more indirect based on the provided annotation. Basement-membrane integrity and extracellular matrix anchoring are important determinants of myocardial structure, vascular stability, and interstitial remodeling. Heart failure is accompanied by substantial changes in matrix composition and tissue architecture, and proteins that stabilize matrix-basement membrane interactions may influence ventricular stiffness and microvascular integrity. PRELP therefore stands out as a potentially informative extracellular matrix component, particularly in forms of heart failure where fibrosis and structural remodeling are dominant features. Its relevance is more indirect than that of major signaling molecules such as TGFBR2 or VEGFA, but it fits well within the broader remodeling framework.

Along similar lines, VCAN is relevant to heart failure because proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix remodeling is a hallmark of both inflammatory and fibrotic cardiac disease. By linking cells to the extracellular matrix and influencing motility, growth, and differentiation, VCAN may contribute to fibroblast behavior, inflammatory-cell trafficking, and tissue organization during adverse remodeling. Its binding to hyaluronic acid is notable because hyaluronan-rich matrix environments often accompany tissue injury, inflammation, and fibrosis. In the failing heart, such matrix changes can alter mechanical properties, cell signaling, and reparative responses. VCAN therefore represents a plausible matrix regulator with potential importance in structural and inflammatory aspects of heart-failure pathogenesis.

Shifting from extracellular matrix remodeling to inflammatory injury, MPO is highly relevant to heart failure because oxidative stress and inflammatory leukocyte activation are major drivers of myocardial injury, endothelial dysfunction, and adverse remodeling. The generation of hypochlorous acid and related oxidants can amplify tissue damage, impair nitric oxide bioavailability, and promote vascular dysfunction, all of which are implicated in heart-failure progression. Although the annotation also notes a potentially protective role through generation of a form of alpha-1-microglobulin that limits low-density lipoprotein oxidation, the dominant biological theme is strong oxidative and inflammatory activity. In clinical cardiovascular research, MPO has often been linked to vascular injury and inflammatory burden, making it a plausible contributor to the oxidative-inflammatory axis of heart failure. Thus, MPO stands out as a mechanistically relevant marker and mediator of disease-related stress responses.[PubMed:11593004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11593004) 

Finally, returning to the interface between angiogenesis and remodeling, CCN3 is potentially important in heart failure because it combines regulation of angiogenesis, differentiation, and stress-responsive signaling. Its inhibitory effects on endothelial proliferation and angiogenic sprouting suggest that it could influence microvascular adaptation in the failing heart, where insufficient angiogenesis can exacerbate ischemia and remodeling. The possible enhancement of HIF1A function is also noteworthy, as hypoxia signaling is central to cardiac adaptation under pressure overload or ischemic stress. In addition, CCN family proteins often participate in extracellular signaling networks that shape fibrosis, cell survival, and tissue remodeling. Although the provided annotation is not heart-specific, CCN3 stands out as a plausible regulator of vascular and remodeling responses relevant to heart-failure pathophysiology.

### endopeptidase activity (GO:0004175) 

Endopeptidase activity refers to the catalytic cleavage of internal alpha-peptide bonds within polypeptide chains, distinguishing these enzymes from exopeptidases that remove terminal residues. This biochemical function is executed by several protease families, including serine, cysteine, aspartyl, metalloproteases, and threonine proteases, and it operates in intracellular, lysosomal, membrane-associated, extracellular, and circulating compartments. Through controlled protein processing, endopeptidases regulate peptide hormone maturation and degradation, receptor activation, extracellular matrix turnover, inflammatory mediator generation, antigen processing, and execution of programmed cell death. The biological consequences of endopeptidase activity are therefore highly context dependent: it may maintain homeostasis by removing damaged proteins and modulating signaling peptides, but excessive, misplaced, or dysregulated endopeptidase activity can promote tissue injury, maladaptive remodeling, and cell loss. The publications provided illustrate this breadth of function, ranging from microbial and intestinal disease contexts to lysosomal protease biology and cardiovascular therapeutics. In the setting of heart failure, the most directly relevant aspect of this pathway is that several clinically and biologically important enzymes with endopeptidase function participate in neurohormonal regulation, proteolytic signaling, and apoptosis-related cascades that shape cardiac performance and disease progression.  

Against this broad functional background, the relationship between endopeptidase activity and heart failure is supported most clearly by studies of cardiovascular proteolytic systems that regulate neurohormonal balance and cardiomyocyte survival. Angiotensin converting enzyme is a dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase within the broader protease network that processes vasoactive peptides, and its inhibition with captopril produced rapid hemodynamic improvement in refractory congestive heart failure, including reduced arterial pressure, reduced filling pressures, increased cardiac index, and suppression of aldosterone and noradrenaline, thereby demonstrating that peptide-processing protease activity is mechanistically important in heart failure pathophysiology and therapeutically tractable (PubMed:87679). Similarly, neprilysin, a membrane metallopeptidase with endopeptidase activity that degrades natriuretic peptides and other vasoactive mediators, is directly implicated in heart failure treatment; inhibition of neprilysin in combination with angiotensin receptor blockade was developed specifically because limiting this endopeptidase augments endogenous compensatory peptide systems and improves outcomes in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (PubMed:27274196). Beyond hemodynamic peptide regulation, protease-dependent cell death pathways are also relevant. In failing human hearts, increased activity of caspase eight and cleavage of caspase three were observed together with activation of endogenous antiapoptotic restraints, indicating that proteolytic execution machinery is engaged during heart failure even when terminal apoptosis is partly contained; this finding places endopeptidase-like apoptotic protease activity within the molecular landscape of failing myocardium (PubMed:19234503). Additional support for a broader proteolytic contribution comes from work showing that cathepsin B possesses endopeptidase activity across acidic and neutral conditions, a property consistent with potential activity in lysosomal, cytosolic, and extracellular environments relevant to stressed or remodeling myocardium, although this study was not heart-failure specific (PubMed:35981509). Taken together, the provided literature suggests that endopeptidase activity may be related to heart failure through at least two major mechanisms: first, by controlling the generation and degradation of vasoactive peptides that determine preload, afterload, neurohormonal activation, and cardiac efficiency; and second, by participating in intracellular proteolytic cascades linked to cardiomyocyte injury, apoptosis signaling, and myocardial remodeling. Thus, while the generic pathway term is broad, the publications support the view that dysregulated or therapeutically targeted endopeptidase activity is likely to represent an important component of heart failure biology and treatment.[PubMed:87679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/87679) [PubMed:27274196](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27274196) [PubMed:19234503](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19234503) [PubMed:35981509](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35981509) 

Building on this literature-based rationale, the enrichment results provide a complementary systems-level view of how broadly this pathway may be represented in heart failure. There were 57 heart failure-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of endopeptidase activity, a functional category centered on the catalytic cleavage of internal alpha-peptide bonds within polypeptide chains and biologically relevant to proteolytic signaling, extracellular matrix turnover, neurohormonal peptide processing, inflammatory mediator generation, and programmed cell death in the failing heart. In a disease setting characterized by progressive ventricular dysfunction, maladaptive remodeling, and sustained neurohormonal stress, an enrichment signal supported by 57 proteins indicates that proteolytic regulation is not represented by an isolated enzyme subset, but instead reflects a broad and coordinated molecular layer with potential impact across intracellular, membrane-associated, extracellular, lysosomal, and circulating compartments. This scale of representation is consistent with the central role of endopeptidase-dependent mechanisms in heart failure pathobiology, where altered cleavage of signaling peptides, receptors, matrix components, and death-related substrates can influence myocardial contractility, fibrosis, inflammation, and cardiomyocyte survival. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 57 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/2a4515ec-57f9-40f8-97f3-ac08e82ab521.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=78A69A99065EF49D)

To move from pathway-level enrichment to more specific biological interpretation, the significant proteins identified in this analysis are introduced below in turn. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
PCSK9 is one of the strongest candidates in this list for relevance to heart failure because it directly controls lipid metabolism through degradation of LDLR and related receptors, thereby influencing circulating LDL cholesterol levels and the progression of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Atherosclerosis and ischemic heart disease are major upstream causes of heart failure, especially heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Beyond systemic lipid regulation, the involvement of PCSK9 in receptor trafficking, APOB handling, and ENaC regulation suggests broader effects on cardiometabolic homeostasis, sodium balance, and vascular biology, all of which are highly pertinent to heart failure pathogenesis and progression. Its receptor targets, particularly LRP1 and related lipoprotein receptors, also intersect with myocardial remodeling and cell survival pathways. Therefore, PCSK9 stands out as a mechanistically important protein linking dyslipidemia, vascular disease, and downstream heart failure risk.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

In a related but distinct way, several additional proteins in the enriched set appear to converge on remodeling, stress adaptation, and inflammatory signaling. SFRP1 is highly relevant to heart failure because dysregulated Wnt/beta-catenin signaling is a well-recognized contributor to cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, vascular remodeling, and maladaptive repair after myocardial injury. As a secreted antagonist/modulator of Wnt signaling that lowers beta-catenin activity, SFRP1 may influence fibroblast activation, vascular smooth muscle proliferation, and angiogenic responses, all of which are central components of the transition from cardiac injury to chronic heart failure. Its reported antiproliferative effects on vascular cells further support a role in vascular remodeling, which is relevant both to ischemic heart failure and to pressure-overload states. Although the entry does not provide direct heart-specific evidence, the mechanistic overlap between Wnt pathway regulation and myocardial remodeling makes SFRP1 one of the most biologically compelling proteins in this set.  

Extending this theme of cellular stress responses, PDIA3 is potentially important in heart failure because it links two processes that are central to cardiac disease biology: endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis and immune activation. Heart failure is associated with chronic cellular stress, including oxidative stress and unfolded protein responses in cardiomyocytes and vascular cells. A disulfide isomerase/chaperone such as PDIA3 may therefore influence the ability of stressed cells to maintain protein quality control. In parallel, its essential role in MHC class I antigen presentation suggests relevance to inflammatory and immune-mediated mechanisms of cardiac injury, including myocarditis, post-ischemic inflammation, and persistent immune activation during heart failure progression. Thus, PDIA3 stands out as a plausible mediator at the intersection of proteotoxic stress and adaptive immunity in failing myocardium.  

Along similar lines, innate immune amplification may also be relevant in this pathway context. CFD is notable because complement activation is increasingly recognized as an important driver of inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and tissue injury in cardiovascular disease and heart failure. By acting as an essential protease in the alternative complement pathway, CFD can amplify innate immune responses that may contribute to myocardial damage, adverse remodeling, and microvascular dysfunction. Complement-mediated inflammation is relevant in ischemic injury, myocarditis, and chronic heart failure, where persistent low-grade immune activation is associated with worse outcomes. Therefore, CFD is mechanistically linked to inflammatory pathways that can exacerbate cardiac dysfunction and remodeling.  

A further extension of this inflammatory and vascular remodeling framework is provided by ADAM9. ADAM9 is relevant to heart failure because its substrate profile includes several endothelial and vascular signaling molecules with direct importance for angiogenesis, vascular permeability, inflammation, and endothelial integrity. Cleavage of TEK, KDR, EPHB4, VCAM1, and CDH5 suggests that ADAM9 could modulate vascular remodeling and leukocyte-endothelial interactions, both of which are central to cardiac injury responses and chronic heart failure progression. In failing hearts, maladaptive angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammatory cell recruitment contribute to fibrosis and impaired perfusion. Through its effects on adhesion molecules and receptor shedding, ADAM9 may influence these processes and thereby affect the myocardial microenvironment.[PubMed:19273593](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19273593) [PubMed:9920899](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9920899) [PubMed:10825303](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10825303) 

Consistent with the importance of inflammatory remodeling, PRTN3 is also of interest in heart failure because it combines matrix-degrading activity with regulation of neutrophil trafficking and inflammatory signaling. Extracellular matrix turnover is a defining feature of adverse cardiac remodeling, and proteases capable of degrading elastin, fibronectin, laminin, and collagens may contribute to structural changes in the myocardium and vasculature. In addition, neutrophil activation and transendothelial migration are important in acute myocardial injury and can shape subsequent remodeling that predisposes to heart failure. The ability of PRTN3 to modulate endothelial barrier function and inflammatory signaling through PAR2-related pathways further supports its relevance to vascular inflammation and tissue injury in cardiovascular disease.[PubMed:2033050](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2033050) [PubMed:28240246](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28240246) [PubMed:3198760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3198760) [PubMed:23202369](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23202369) [PubMed:22266279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22266279) [PubMed:36302784](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36302784) 

From inflammatory proteases, the discussion then shifts toward antiviral and immune-regulatory mechanisms that may also intersect with myocardial injury. BST2 is potentially relevant to heart failure primarily through immune and inflammatory mechanisms. Viral infection is an established cause of myocarditis and subsequent dilated cardiomyopathy, and BST2 is a broad antiviral restriction factor active against many enveloped viruses. Its capacity to regulate interferon feedback through LILRA4/ILT7 and to influence NF-kappa-B signaling suggests that it may shape the intensity and duration of antiviral inflammation, which can determine whether myocardial infection resolves or progresses to chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy and heart failure. The additional effect on MMP14/MMP15-related growth and migration may also connect BST2 to tissue remodeling processes. Thus, BST2 stands out as a plausible mediator linking antiviral defense, innate immune regulation, and remodeling-associated pathways relevant to heart failure.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

In addition to these immune-centered candidates, extracellular matrix-associated proteins may also contribute to the structural dimension of heart failure progression. ITIH3 is relevant to heart failure because hyaluronan is an important extracellular matrix component involved in inflammation, edema, tissue repair, and fibrosis. Regulation of hyaluronan localization and turnover can influence matrix organization and cell-matrix signaling in injured tissues, including the heart. Since adverse extracellular matrix remodeling is a key determinant of ventricular stiffness, fibrosis, and progression to heart failure, proteins that modulate hyaluronan biology may have meaningful mechanistic importance. Although the evidence here is indirect, ITIH3 stands out as a matrix-associated factor with plausible relevance to cardiac remodeling and interstitial changes in heart failure.  

A related interface between tissue injury and systemic complications is suggested by AMBP. AMBP is potentially connected to heart failure through coagulation and inflammatory protease regulation. Heart failure is frequently accompanied by a prothrombotic state, endothelial dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory activation. A protein capable of inhibiting factor Xa and prothrombin activation may influence thrombosis risk, while inhibition of mast cell proteases is also notable because mast cells contribute to fibrosis, matrix remodeling, and inflammatory signaling in cardiovascular disease. Thus, AMBP may be relevant at the interface between coagulation, inflammation, and remodeling, all of which shape heart failure progression and complications.  

Finally, the remaining candidates point toward growth factor activation and reparative signaling as another possible layer of relevance within the enriched pathway. SPINT1 is of interest because it regulates protease systems linked to hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) activation and epithelial or tissue remodeling. HGF signaling is broadly associated with tissue repair, angiogenesis, anti-fibrotic responses, and cytoprotection, processes that are highly relevant in the injured heart. By inhibiting HGF activator and related proteases, SPINT1 may indirectly modulate reparative signaling pathways that influence remodeling after cardiac stress or ischemic injury. Although the present annotation is not heart-specific, the mechanistic connection to growth factor activation makes SPINT1 a potentially relevant regulator of pathways implicated in heart failure.[PubMed:9045658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9045658) [PubMed:28710277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28710277) [PubMed:20977675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20977675)  

Closely related to this point, SPINT2 is notable because activation of HGF can influence MAPK signaling, cell survival, tissue repair, and anti-fibrotic pathways. In the context of heart failure, HGF signaling has been implicated in cardioprotection, vascular repair, and modulation of fibrosis. Therefore, a protein that promotes conversion of pro-HGF to active HGF could affect myocardial adaptation to injury and the balance between reparative and maladaptive remodeling. While the current annotation is not directly cardiac, the ability of SPINT2 to regulate growth factor activation and downstream MAPK signaling provides a plausible mechanistic link to heart failure biology.[PubMed:20977675](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20977675) [PubMed:28710277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28710277) [PubMed:34562451](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34562451)
